correctness.rationale: Unital K-algebra automorphisms fix K and preserve the unique maximal ideal V. Square-zero multiplication makes every invertible K-linear map on V extend to an automorphism. Interpolating the pair (v,a1+v) forces the radical part of any two-local map to depend only on v. On V, the pair (v,cv) forces homogeneity with the same c, and independent pairs must stay independent. This permutes projective directions over the finite field; every such permutation with an independent nonzero scale on each direction is two-local by extending independent pairs to bases, or by homogeneity for dependent pairs. Composition gives the stated wreath product and order. The triple (v,w,v+w) forces additivity and hence, with homogeneity and injectivity, invertible K-linearity. When n=1 or (n,q)=(2,2) the two-local group is already GL. Else, scaling just one direction for q>2, or swapping x+y with z for three independent vectors when q=2, violates additivity. These arguments do not require the prime-field hypothesis of the frozen finite checker.
residual_risks: The finite orbit checks complement the proof; they do not extend it to semilinear witnesses, arbitrary rings or nonsplit algebras.

value.rationale: The square-zero family isolates how much local agreement can fail to enforce linearity over finite fields. It gives the full discrepancy group rather than just examples and pins down the small-field exception and exact two-to-three evaluation boundary. This is a useful classification for the natural first radical-square-zero test family, beyond the elementary identification of the ordinary automorphism group or computation of a tiny example.
